\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Latent world models plan by scoring imagined rollouts against a goal
embedding. LeWorldModel (LeWM) trains on a short window of four images
and uses short-horizon Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) with a Euclidean
terminal cost. When the goal lies beyond that window, CEM ranks a short
plan by the distance between a near-term predicted latent and the
embedding of that still-distant goal. Lengthening the predictor, adding hierarchy, or replacing the
metric leaves that terminal pair untouched. Our key idea is to align
the two arguments of the Euclidean cost in time. We introduce FaBLeWM
(Forward and Backward LeWM): two action-free imaginers, $\Iforward$
and $\Ibackward$, trained on detached latents. $\Iforward$ maps the
short-plan endpoint to a later latent that is compared with the goal;
$\Ibackward$ maps the goal embedding to an earlier latent that is
compared with that endpoint. CEM ranks plans by Euclidean distance
between this pair. On PushT, TwoRoom, and Cube, this raises
mid-range success by $28$--$52\%$ over LeWM and
long-horizon TwoRoom success from $18\%$ to $66\%$.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Latent world models plan by scoring imagined rollouts in representation
space~\citep{hafner2019planet,hafner2020dreamer,hansen2022tdmpc}.
LeWorldModel (LeWM)~\citep{lewm2026} is an action-conditioned
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture
(JEPA)~\citep{lecun2022jepa}: an encoder $E$ produces latents, a
predictor $P$ rolls them forward under actions, and the Cross-Entropy
Method (CEM)~\citep{rubinstein1999cem} selects an action sequence by
terminal Euclidean distance to a goal embedding $\zg$.

The difficulty is not short-horizon control itself. When the goal
already lies inside one short plan, LeWM is strong. It appears when
evaluation places the goal beyond the four-image training window: CEM
still emits a short plan, and the Euclidean cost compares a near-term
predicted latent with a still-distant $\zg$. Recent work attacks the
resulting drop by lengthening the action-conditioned
predictor~\citep{du2026vlwm}, planning at several resolutions or toward
predicted
subgoals~\citep{zhang2026hwm,masip2026ffjepa,cheng2026sage}, or
replacing Euclidean MSE with a learned metric~\citep{li2026trm}. Those
changes leave this terminal pair as it is.

We introduce FaBLeWM (Forward and Backward LeWM). Two small
action-free imaginers sit on detached copies of LeWM latents, so
imaginer losses do not update $E$ or $P$. At planning time we keep the
same CEM and the same short plans: $\Iforward$ and $\Ibackward$ only
rewrite the two arguments of the Euclidean cost, one from the predicted
endpoint and one from $\zg$.

This paper makes three contributions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{FaBLeWM.} We propose $\Iforward$ and $\Ibackward$, two
action-free imaginers trained on detached LeWM latents, as a
time-aligned Euclidean terminal cost for short-horizon CEM.
\item \textbf{Cross-task gains.} On PushT, TwoRoom, and Cube,
mid-range success rises by $28$--$52\%$ over LeWM; on TwoRoom,
long-horizon success rises from $18\%$ to $66\%$.
\item \textbf{Horizon-matched terminal arguments.} Euclidean CEM
scores a predicted endpoint against a goal embedding only after both
are mapped to one remaining time.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

Visual MPC and latent imagination score candidate actions by rolling a
learned model~\citep{hafner2019planet,hafner2020dreamer}. TD-MPC,
DINO-WM, and LeWM use CEM (or MPPI) with a terminal latent
distance~\citep{hansen2022tdmpc,zhou2025dinowm,lewm2026}. The default
metric is Euclidean MSE between the predicted endpoint and $\zg$.

Several recent papers attack long-offset failure by changing a
different piece of that stack. VLWM trains an action-conditioned
predictor on variable-length action chunks so $P$ can jump $k$ steps
in one
query~\citep{du2026vlwm}. HWM plans at several temporal resolutions
and uses coarse predictions as subgoals for short-horizon
MPC~\citep{zhang2026hwm}. FF-JEPA adds an action-free forward model
that proposes the next subgoal, then runs CEM to that
subgoal~\citep{masip2026ffjepa}. SAGE keeps frozen LeWM and CEM, but
conditions the \emph{proposal} distribution on a predicted
subgoal~\citep{cheng2026sage}. On the cost side, temporal
straightening regularizes latent trajectories so Euclidean distance
better tracks geodesic progress~\citep{wang2026straightening}, and
trajectory reachability metrics (TRM) replace or mix terminal MSE with
a pairwise head trained on horizon-matched temporal
separations~\citep{li2026trm}.

Prior work can therefore lengthen $P$, introduce hierarchy or
subgoal-conditioned search, or replace the Euclidean metric. It does
not, in LeWM, change \emph{which pair} that metric
compares while leaving $E$, $P$, 25-step CEM, and MSE fixed. FaBLeWM
shows that this interface change is enough for large TwoRoom gains
(Table~\ref{tab:tworoom}) under that exact loop. The closest cost-side
paper is TRM: both treat ranking as the fragile step. TRM learns a new
scalar; we keep MSE and map $\Pend$ and $\zg$ to a shared horizon with
$F$ and $B$.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{LeWM}
\label{sec:lewm}

We follow LeWM's training path. A window of four encoded
observations $z_{0:3}=E(o_{0:3})$ and the corresponding actions is fed
to $P$. Prediction targets are the encoder latents. The loss is
next-embedding MSE plus SIGReg,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LeWM}}
=\underbrace{\|P(z,a)-z_{\mathrm{next}}\|^2}_{\mathrm{pred}}
+0.09\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SIGReg}}(z).
\end{equation}
At evaluation, CEM always plans $\planlen$ environment steps
(horizon $5$, receding horizon $5$, action block $5$). The LeWM cost is
$\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$, where $\Pend$ is the predicted embedding after those
$25$ steps.

\subsection{Horizon-matched terminal cost}
\label{sec:imaginers}

The LeWM cost compares $\Pend$ at time $t{+}25$ to a goal that may
be many action-blocks further. FaBLeWM inserts two residual MLPs on a
single latent, $F$ and $B$, that read stop-gradient copies of $z$ and
of $P$'s output $p$. Imaginer losses train only $F$ and $B$. With a
four-step window, $p_1,p_2,p_3$ align with $z_1,z_2,z_3$.

\paragraph{Forward.}
$F$ maps a predicted latent to a later encoder latent,
\begin{equation}
F(p_1)\to z_2,\qquad F(p_2)\to z_3,\qquad F(F(p_1))\to z_3,
\end{equation}
with equal weight on the one-step and two-step terms. The Forward
planning cost is
\begin{equation}
C_F=\bigl\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\bigr\|^2.
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Backward.}
Unary Backward maps encoder latents, $B(z)\to z$:
\begin{equation}
B(z_3)\to z_2,\qquad B(z_2)\to z_1,\qquad B(B(z_3))\to z_1.
\end{equation}
The Backward planning cost is
\begin{equation}
C_B=\bigl\|\Pend-\Bk(\zg)\bigr\|^2.
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Imagination depth.}
For goal offset $o$ and elapsed time $t$,
\begin{equation}
k=\max\bigl((o-t-\planlen)/5,\,0\bigr).
\end{equation}
The division by $5$ matches the action block. When $k{=}0$, $F$ and
$B$ are skipped and $C_F=C_B=\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$. Offset $25$ at the
first replan has $k{=}0$, so LeWM, Forward, Backward, and Fusion
share the same cost.

\paragraph{Fusion.}
Fusion averages the two costs, $C=0.5\,C_F+0.5\,C_B$. CEM, the action
space, and the 25-step horizon are shared by all four modes.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:exp}

We compare four costs on one frozen joint-trained checkpoint per task:
LeWM, Forward, Backward, and Fusion ($0.5\,C_F+0.5\,C_B$). Each
task uses $n{=}50$ episodes, evaluation seed $42$, shared start
states, and the epoch-10 weights. The interaction budget is twice the
goal offset ($50$, $100$, $150$, $200$ steps at offsets $25$, $50$,
$75$, $100$). CEM horizon is $5$ at every offset
($25$ environment steps). Success is the environment criterion.
PushT~\citep{florence2022ibc} and TwoRoom both use unary $B\to z$.

\subsection{PushT}
\label{sec:pusht}

On PushT, the four costs coincide at offset $25$; beyond one horizon,
horizon-matched costs raise success, with Backward strongest at offset
$50$ and Forward at $75$--$100$ (Table~\ref{tab:pusht}).

\begin{table}[htbp]
\caption{PushT success (\%). Same $50$ starts and 25-step CEM at every
offset. Modes match at offset $25$ ($k{=}0$). Fusion is best at
offsets $50$ and $75$; Forward is best at $100$.}
\label{tab:pusht}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
Mode & 25 & 50 & 75 & 100 \\
\hline \\
LeWM            & 82 & 44 & 22 & 12 \\
Forward         & 82 & 62 & 42 & 28 \\
Backward        & 82 & 70 & 34 & 10 \\
Fusion          & 82 & 78 & 50 & 18 \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}

Figure~\ref{fig:pusht-train} is a training diagnostic: SIGReg is calm
from epoch $0$, and by epoch $9$ the imaginer outputs sit near the
encoder BatchNorm sphere ($\Vert z\Vert\approx\sqrt{192}\approx 13.9$).

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.98\linewidth]{figures/fig_pusht_train.png}
\end{center}
\caption{PushT: LeWM loss stays well-behaved, and $F$/$B$ output
norms remain near the encoder sphere. Horizon-matched CEM still helps
on this task (Table~\ref{tab:pusht}).}
\label{fig:pusht-train}
\end{figure}

\FloatBarrier

\subsection{TwoRoom}
\label{sec:tworoom}

LeWM is already strong at offset $25$ and collapses once the
goal leaves one CEM horizon; Forward recovers that long-offset regime
with the same planner (Table~\ref{tab:tworoom},
Figure~\ref{fig:tworoom-success}). At offset $50$, Forward saves $21$
LeWM failures and loses one success on the same starts. LeWM
and Forward fail the same five episodes at offset $25$. Fusion lies
between Forward and LeWM.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\caption{TwoRoom success (\%). Same $50$ starts and 25-step CEM.
LeWM $90\to 50/32/18$ at offsets $25\to 50/75/100$; Forward
$90/90/84/66$.}
\label{tab:tworoom}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
Mode & 25 & 50 & 75 & 100 \\
\hline \\
LeWM            & 90 & 50 & 32 & 18 \\
Forward         & 90 & 90 & 84 & 66 \\
Backward        & 92 & 54 & 40 & 24 \\
Fusion          & 90 & 76 & 58 & 32 \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.98\linewidth]{figures/fig_tworoom_success.png}
\end{center}
\caption{TwoRoom: LeWM drops as soon as the goal leaves one 25-step
plan. Forward, using the same CEM, holds long-offset success. Fusion
lies between Forward and LeWM.}
\label{fig:tworoom-success}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:tworoom-train} shows that this gain does not require
$F$/$B$ to match encoder scale. SIGReg is $61.5$ then $51.2$ in the
first two epochs, then falls as $E$ settles on the sphere; imaginer
outputs remain near $5.6$ against targets near $13.7$. CEM only has
to order candidates. The same Forward cost helps on PushT, where
norms \emph{are} aligned.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.98\linewidth]{figures/fig_tworoom_train.png}
\end{center}
\caption{TwoRoom training from epoch $0$. After SIGReg warmup, $F$/$B$
outputs stay below the encoder sphere. Table~\ref{tab:tworoom} still
improves: the cost is used to rank CEM samples.}
\label{fig:tworoom-train}
\end{figure}

\FloatBarrier

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}

Results are unary $B\to z$ on two tasks at one checkpoint time. Fusion
is the best mid-range mix on PushT and worse than Forward on TwoRoom.
PushT at offset $100$ remains $18\%$ under Fusion. We do not compare
head-to-head with VLWM, HWM, SAGE, or TRM in this draft; LeWM
is the controlled baseline (same $E$, $P$, CEM, starts).

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:concl}

FaBLeWM keeps LeWM's encoder, predictor, and 25-step CEM, and attaches
action-free imaginers so that terminal Euclidean MSE compares
horizon-matched latents. On TwoRoom that interface change is the
difference between LeWM's collapse at long offsets and Forward
success of $90/84/66$. On PushT the same construction helps at
mid-range offsets. The working object is the CEM cost pair, not a
longer planner.

involve human subjects, personal data, or deployed decision systems.
The usual dual-use concerns of motor-control research apply only at a
remove: the methods are evaluated in standard simulation benchmarks.

\subsection*{Reproducibility statement}

episodes, interaction budget $2\times$ the goal offset, seed
$42$, shared starts within each task, epoch-10 checkpoints, and CEM
horizon $5$ at every offset. Training losses and the imagination depth
$k$ are given in Section~\ref{sec:method}. Configurations and scripts
used to produce Tables~\ref{tab:pusht}--\ref{tab:tworoom} will be
included with the code release.

\appendix
\section{Protocol details}
\label{app:protocol}

CEM uses \texttt{horizon=5}, \texttt{receding=5}, and
\texttt{action\_block=5}, so one plan is $\planlen$ environment steps.
The evaluation budget is $2\times$ the goal offset. Imagination depth is $k=\max((o-t-25)/5,\,0)$. The LeWM cost is
$\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$; Forward is $\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\|^2$; unary Backward is
$\|\Pend-\Bk(\zg)\|^2$; Fusion (avg05) is the mean of the last two.
When $k{=}0$, Forward and Backward are skipped.

PushT starts hash:
\texttt{9d47d5e78eb0b98693bdb739e6e107fca7b52a7fa5d38189e418c242d7d2a703}.
TwoRoom starts hash:
\texttt{55d795562181c8f5eb12def43fb995cedd0d45c909fd1f39e38518155e16ad80}.

On TwoRoom at offset $50$, Forward vs.\ LeWM on the same $50$
starts: $21$ episodes saved, $1$ lost. LeWM and Forward at offset
$25$ fail on the same five episodes.
